fanoutqa_002568.x:
Carmelo Anthony :: Professional career :: New York Knicks (2011–2017) :: 2015–16 season :: chunk_0021
On January 20, 2016, in the Knicks' 118–111 overtime win against the Jazz, Anthony recorded 30 points, seven rebounds and nine assists, while passing [Larry Bird](/wiki/Larry_Bird "Larry Bird") for 31st place in career points scored.[[167]](#cite_note-167)[[168]](#cite_note-168) On January 21, Anthony was voted as starter for the [2016 NBA All-Star Game](/wiki/2016_NBA_All-Star_Game "2016 NBA All-Star Game").[[169]](#cite_note-169) In the All-Star game Anthony recorded 11 points, 6 rebounds and 1 block in the East's 196–173 loss to the West.[[170]](#cite_note-170) On January 23, Anthony moved past [Gary Payton](/wiki/Gary_Payton "Gary Payton") as the league's 30th all-time career scoring leader in a 97–84 loss to the [Charlotte Hornets](/wiki/Charlotte_Hornets "Charlotte Hornets").[[171]](#cite_note-171) In the team's 128–97 victory against the Phoenix Suns on March 9, 2016, Anthony scored 23 points with 7 rebounds as he passed another NBA legend, [Clyde Drexler](/wiki/Clyde_Drexler "Clyde Drexler"), in the career scoring list moving up to No. 29.[[172]](#cite_note-172)

While Anthony ended the season with an average of 21.8 ppg (1,573 points in 72 games), below his 25.2 ppg average entering the season, he set a career-high 4.2 apg average (299 assists in 72 games),[[173]](#cite_note-173) the first and only time that he averaged over 4.0 apg in his career.[[174]](#cite_note-174)

fanoutqa_024328.x:
Monterey Bay :: chunk_0000
[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3e/Monterey_Bay_Map_%28smaller%29.png/330px-Monterey_Bay_Map_%28smaller%29.png)](/wiki/File:Monterey_Bay_Map_(smaller).png)

Map of the Monterey Bay Area, depicting roads, urban areas, major rivers, and forested and grassy areas

**Monterey Bay** is a bay of the [Pacific Ocean](/wiki/Pacific_Ocean "Pacific Ocean") located on the coast of the [U.S. state](/wiki/U.S._state "U.S. state") of [California](/wiki/California "California"), south of the [San Francisco Bay Area](/wiki/San_Francisco_Bay_Area "San Francisco Bay Area"). [San Francisco](/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco") itself is farther north along the coast, by about 75 miles (120 km), accessible via [CA 1](/wiki/California_State_Route_1 "California State Route 1") and [US 101](/wiki/U.S._Route_101_in_California "U.S. Route 101 in California").

[Santa Cruz](/wiki/Santa_Cruz,_California "Santa Cruz, California") is located at the north end of the bay, and [Monterey](/wiki/Monterey,_California "Monterey, California") is on the [Monterey Peninsula](/wiki/Monterey_Peninsula "Monterey Peninsula") at the south end. The "**Monterey Bay Area**" is a regional term used to describe the Monterey Bay-adjacent [Central Coast](/wiki/Central_Coast_(California) "Central Coast (California)") communities of [Santa Cruz](/wiki/Santa_Cruz_County,_California "Santa Cruz County, California"), [Monterey](/wiki/Monterey_County,_California "Monterey County, California"), and [San Benito](/wiki/San_Benito_County,_California "San Benito County, California") counties. The three counties, along with Monterey Bay-adjacent cities, collaborate in the Association of Monterey Bay Governments (AMBAG) on regional issues and come together for events like the State of the Region hosted by the Monterey Bay Economic Partnership.

Frances Arnold :: Early life and education :: chunk_0001
Arnold is the daughter of Josephine Inman (née Routheau) and nuclear physicist [William Howard Arnold](/wiki/William_Howard_Arnold_(physicist) "William Howard Arnold (physicist)"), and the granddaughter of Lieutenant General [William Howard Arnold](/wiki/William_Howard_Arnold_(general) "William Howard Arnold (general)").[[5]](#cite_note-5) She has an older brother, Bill, and three younger brothers, Edward, David and Thomas. She grew up in the [Pittsburgh](/wiki/Pittsburgh "Pittsburgh") suburb of [Edgewood](/wiki/Edgewood,_Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania "Edgewood, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania"), and the Pittsburgh neighborhoods of [Shadyside](/wiki/Shadyside_(Pittsburgh) "Shadyside (Pittsburgh)") and [Squirrel Hill](/wiki/Squirrel_Hill_(Pittsburgh) "Squirrel Hill (Pittsburgh)"), graduating from the city's [Taylor Allderdice High School](/wiki/Taylor_Allderdice_High_School "Taylor Allderdice High School") in 1974.[[6]](#cite_note-6) As a high schooler, she hitchhiked to Washington, D.C., to protest the [Vietnam War](/wiki/Vietnam_War "Vietnam War")[[7]](#cite_note-7) and lived on her own, working as a cocktail waitress at a local jazz club and a cab driver.[[8]](#cite_note-:7-8)

The same independence that drove Arnold to move out of her childhood home as a teenager also led to a large volume of absences from school and low grades. In spite of this, she made near perfect scores on standardized tests and was determined to attend Princeton University, the alma mater of her father. She applied as a mechanical engineering major and was accepted.[[9]](#cite_note-:8-9) Arnold's motivation behind studying engineering, as stated in her Nobel Prize interview, was that "[mechanical engineering] was the easiest option and the easiest way to get into Princeton University at the time and I never left".[[10]](#cite_note-10)

Burrell attended the [University of Miami](/wiki/University_of_Miami "University of Miami"), where he won the [Golden Spikes Award](/wiki/Golden_Spikes_Award "Golden Spikes Award") in 1998. On June 2, 1998, he was the [first overall draft pick](/wiki/List_of_first_overall_Major_League_Baseball_draft_picks "List of first overall Major League Baseball draft picks") by the Philadelphia Phillies. After two years in the minor leagues, Burrell was called up by the Phillies in 2000, and he finished fourth in voting for the [National League Rookie of the Year](/wiki/National_League_Rookie_of_the_Year "National League Rookie of the Year") Award. After hitting 27 [home runs](/wiki/Home_runs "Home runs") (HR) in 2001 (the first of eight straight years in which Burrell would hit at least 20), he hit a career-high 37 home runs in 2002 and finished 14th in [NL Most Valuable Player Award](/wiki/National_League_Most_Valuable_Player "National League Most Valuable Player") voting. In 2003, Burrell signed a six-year contract with the Phillies but [batted](/wiki/Batting_average_(baseball) "Batting average (baseball)") a career-low .209, with 21 home runs. In 2004, he batted .257 with 24 home runs but missed several games with a wrist injury. Burrell hit 32 home runs in 2005 and finished seventh in NL MVP Award voting after he set a career high with 117 [runs batted in](/wiki/Runs_batted_in "Runs batted in") (RBI). In 2006, he batted .258, with 29 home runs, and 95 RBI but was benched for a few games due to a slump after April. Burrell batted .256 with 30 home runs in 2007 as the Phillies reached the playoffs for the first time in his career. He hit a home run in the playoffs as the Phillies were swept in the first round. In 2008, Burrell hit 33 home runs as the Phillies reached the playoffs again, winning the [World Series](/wiki/2008_World_Series "2008 World Series").
